sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. Arbiter accepted it: contract stayed and to be read against the keep's rolls, Corvin held for Crowe's assize at Marrowford, Wren not charged but must appear. entries.text: notebook: updated Vantry Hall

You set the psalter on the table and speak plainly, with no flourish and no song. You lay your own part out as bare as the rest: nineteen years at his side, the ledger, the two weeks. Your Persuasion check was a 19. The rehearsal with Kit and the weight of exhaustion cancel out, but a plain tongue doesn't need help.

The hall listens. When you say "I wanted to see for myself whether he'd harmed the houses or only flattered them," a murmur goes through the benches, and nobody there disbelieves it. You slide out the last leaf, the register copy, Elowen's letter, and the ruling you don't have, which you leave unmentioned. The arbiter reads each in turn without a word, and her stylus makes small hard marks on a wax tablet.

It takes the better part of an hour. At the end she sets the tablet down and folds her hands.

"Here is what this hall finds," she says. "The Dray–Vantry contract is stayed, and will be read against the keep's rolls and Sir Corwen's own steward before any seal is set. The clerk in black gloves is held for the keep's justice, and his case with him. Corvin Tallowmere is held in this hall's cellar until Dame Crowe's assize at Marrowford at month's end, and will be sent under guard." She looks at you over her spectacles. "You, mistress, took what was not yours, and kept it, and then did what you could to put it right at some cost to yourself. The hall does not charge you. You will be asked to appear before Dame Crowe, and you will go."

Sir Corwen stands. For a moment you think he will say something hard. Instead he bows to you, stiffly, from the neck, as a proud man does when it costs him. "The Dray name is cleaner for it," he says. "Come to the keep when this is done. There is a bed, and a purse owed, I think, to whoever returned my daughter her choice." Isaude's eyes are bright, and her smile is real.

The arbiter lifts a hand. "The cellar, as I promised. A quarter hour, a guard at the door, and the lady Kit beside you if you wish."

It is twenty to three, and the hall is breaking up around you in a buzz of voices. Down a short stair behind the guard's key, in the dark, Corvin Tallowmere is waiting. He asked for you by name. You've a commission-paper that says he knows where your mother's lamp-staff lies. Your spells are spent, you are still exhausted, and you're three days from a bed that won't be borrowed.

What does Wren do?

Sir Corwen stands. "She stays under my roof if she wants it," he says gruffly. "Or the keep's, if the Vantry won't have her." He doesn't look at you as he says it. Isaude does, and she smiles.

You sleep through the afternoon with your boots steaming by the fire. The storm wears itself thin against the shutters, and Kit's snoring keeps time with it. Sleep like this isn't a long rest. Under it is written: *Reedhithe Shrine-House, keeper Tamsin Orle. Two days upriver of Saltmarsh by the water road. Elowen left the child with her. Fifteen years gone this autumn.* Below that, in a smaller hand: *I paid her thirty marks and a promise. She may not forgive either.*

You read it by the lamp, then lay it beside Elowen's letter and the strip from the staff. Neither names a place except the Gullspit light, so there's nothing to match. But *safe among people who will love her* is what Brann said Elowen told him, and a shrine-house keeper fits that. You turn the sheet over and hold it to the flame, and your Investigation check is an 8 (disadvantage again). It reads as a plain, honest map, but you can't say whether it's honest or just very good. The hand is steady, the ink old, and the lie, if there is one, doesn't show.

Kit has woken and is eating cold stew with her usual attention. "Two days upriver," she says. "That's back toward Marrowford, near enough. Assize is at month's end." She looks at you. "Or the spit, for the foot. Or the arbiter, for Aldous. Pick."

Your options at supper, as I see them:
- Go to Reedhithe by the water road. It's two days up, and then Marrowford for the assize is on the way back.
- Fetch the reliquary from Brann first when the weather clears, then go.
- Wait here a few days for the riders' answers about Aldous, and use the time to rest properly and let the exhaustion wear off.

It is six in the evening. What does Wren decide?

You sleep like a stone. The rain thins to a drip somewhere past four and the fire sinks to red. When Pell raps on the doorframe at dusk, Kit is already awake, sitting on her bedroll and oiling her shield-strap. Your exhaustion hasn't lifted: a few hours' nap is no long rest, and that has to wait for the small hours.

Pell hands over a single folded sheet and stays on the landing, looking at nothing. It is in Corvin's neat copperplate hand, inked in a strict line, without a single flourish. A small map of the lower Marrow. A bend in the river marked *Withy Reach*, a day's ride upriver of Saltmarsh. Below it, in tidy letters:

*The Reedmother's Lantern-House. Green velvet at the door and the altar. The woman was Nan Sedge, a ferryman's widow. I left her eleven silver and a promise. The child was called "Wren" by her already, and no one knew why. Elowen's hand put her there. Mine took her.*

You read it by the lamp. The name of the place isn't in your mother's letter or the strip from the staff, and you can't prove a word of it from paper. But the green velvet sits oddly well. The scrap of ribbon sewn in your cloak hem is the same moss green, and the coffer lay on a bed of the same stuff. A forger would know to put that in. A man telling the truth about a place he'd stood in would too. You can't tell which.

Over supper Pell adds what the hall knows. The Heron's Tithe has not come back to any port the harbour watch can reach, and no rider has returned from Thornhallow yet. He leaves it at that and goes. Kit eats, then says in her dry way: "Withy Reach is on the road back to Marrowford. Nothing's pulling us the other way but the lamp, and that's lit. And the assize is at month's end."

Your options, as you see them: ride upriver to Withy Reach and find Nan Sedge or whoever kept the shrine after her, with Marrowford and Dame Crowe on the same road. Or fetch the reliquary from the spit first, if you want it in your hand. Or wait here for the rider from Thornhallow, which means two or three days. The long rest can finish at about four tomorrow morning if you go to bed now. What does Wren do?

You sleep the afternoon away beside the fire, with Kit snoring across the room and the storm slowly wearing itself out against the shutters. It isn't a long rest. The slots stay at nothing, and the small hours are still ten hours off. You wake a little after six, stiff and warmer, to a knock at the door.

It's Pell, rain-dark and unsmiling, with a folded sheet. "From the cellar," he says. "Not through the clerk. He wrote the whole afternoon and asked for a second sheet." He goes down for supper before you can thank him.

You read it by the lamp. It is a map in Corvin's neat hand, a river bend drawn in a few strokes, and a village marked **Sedgeholm**, a day's ride upriver of Saltmarsh on the lower Marrow. A tiny lantern with a crooked flame sits over a ferry-landing, and beside it:

*The Reed Lantern. A ferry-chapel. Keeper then: Hesper Wynn, a widow who took coin to keep children and ask no questions. Elowen left you with her in the autumn of your fourth year. I paid her twice what Elowen had, and she did not argue. If she's dead, ask the ferryman. I have written nothing here that I didn't see with my own eyes. C.T.*

You check it against what you carry. Elowen's letter and the strip of paper never name a place, only "people who will love her", which doesn't sit comfortably with a woman who took coin. Nothing in them contradicts it, though, and the crooked flame over the door matches the mark in your sketch of the E.A. lantern. It might be true. It might be a very good lie drawn by a man who has made his living from those.

You and Kit share supper in the common room: fish stew again, and bread. She listens to all of it, chewing, and says only "A day up the river" and, a moment later, "Ember's rested."

Your choices are plain enough. You could ride to Sedgeholm to find the Reed Lantern, which is a day's ride upriver, then return for the Gullspit reliquary. It is a little after six. What does Wren decide?

You peel off your wet boots, set them by the fire and sleep like a dropped sack. Kit snores across the room, and the storm wears itself out against the shutters. It isn't a long rest. You'll still have no slots in the morning unless you sleep through the night. But you wake at dusk with your head clearer, and the rain has stopped.

Pell knocks at half past six, as promised. He hands over a single folded sheet, says "Seen by nobody but me," and goes back down the stair before you can thank him.

Corvin's hand is the same careful, looping script that taught you your letters. The map is simple: a line of the lower Marrow, a bend, a little ferry mark and a reed-hut sketch, labelled in neat capitals SEDGEHOLM WAYSHRINE. A day and a half upriver of Saltmarsh by the river road, he notes, below Thornhallow. Under it: *Edda Marsh. Broad, one-eyed, keeps bees. If she is dead, ask the ferryman. Autumn, the year you were four. I paid her eleven silver more than Elowen had. I have written nothing here that I know to be false. — C.* There is a small drawn lantern at the foot.

You check it against what you carry. Elowen's letter and the strip don't mention Sedgeholm or Edda by name. The Wick-House paper and Ysolde point you only at the Gullspit light, which is done. But the route lies along the old road-priest circuit your mother must have walked, and a Lantern-Bearer wayshrine on a ferry is exactly where a priest with a fevering secret and a small child would stop. It fits. Whether it is true, or a place where Corvin wants you to go, is something you can't settle from a page.

Kit sits up, rubs her face and reads it over your shoulder with a dry grunt. "Sedgeholm's on the way to Thornhallow," she says. "Past it, anyway." Supper arrives, fish stew again. The arbiter owes you a sealed copy of the judgment, Dame Crowe's assize is at the end of the month, and Corvin has to be brought to Marrowford alive. Your reliquary is in the lamp on the spit, and Brann is minding it. A rider to Lord Edric and Osric won't be back for a couple of days.

You have no slots, one Bardic Inspiration, and a long rest still owed until the small hours. What does Wren decide over supper?
